summary: Defines a DHCPv6 option that lets a server tell clients which quadrant of the local MAC address space to use, following the IEEE Structured Local Address Plan (SLAP) introduced in IEEE Std 802c. This helps keep automatically assigned local MAC addresses organized.

eli5.summary: The set of locally made hardware names is split into four zones. This lets a helper tell each computer which zone to pick its name from.

subtitle: A DHCPv6 option that lets a client or relay say which IEEE local MAC address quadrant it prefers.

tldr.problem: IEEE 802c splits the local MAC address space into four quadrants with different assignment rules, but a DHCPv6 client or relay had no way to tell the server which quadrant it wants.
tldr.mechanism: The QUAD option (OPTION_SLAP_QUAD, code 140) carries pairs of a quadrant identifier and a preference value, and the server uses them to order its choice of address pool.
tldr.outcome: A client or relay can steer which kind of local MAC address it receives under RFC 8947. It is a Proposed Standard and has not been obsoleted or updated.

today: RFC 8948 is a Proposed Standard published in December 2020, and is not obsoleted or updated by any other RFC. It works together with RFC 8947, which defines the IA_LL and LLADDR options it builds on.

sections.title: Local MAC Address Quadrants
sections.content:
Half of the 48-bit MAC address space is reserved for local use (the U/L bit is 1). In 2017 IEEE published Std 802c, which defines an optional Structured Local Address Plan (SLAP) with four regions called quadrants. Quadrant 01 holds Extended Local Identifiers (ELI), based on a 24-bit Company ID. Quadrant 11 holds Standard Assigned Identifiers (SAI), assigned by an IEEE 802 protocol. Quadrant 00 holds Administratively Assigned Identifiers (AAI), assigned locally. Quadrant 10 is reserved for future use.

RFC 8947 lets a DHCPv6 server allocate local MAC addresses. This document adds extensions so that a DHCPv6 client or relay can indicate a preferred SLAP quadrant, and the server may then allocate from the quadrant requested.
sections.eli5: Imagine four colored buckets of name tags, each with its own rules. This RFC lets you ask the office for a tag from a particular bucket.

sections.title: Why a Preference Is Useful
sections.content:
The RFC gives two application scenarios.

For Wi-Fi devices, two cases matter. IoT devices may boot with a temporary MAC address used only to reach a DHCP server, and any quadrant could do, but ELI or SAI may suit when the device should use the vendor's Company ID. For privacy, devices may use local random addresses that change when they join a different network, and AAI is probably the best fit because the address need not survive moving between networks.

For hypervisors in large data centers, a VM that may be migrated to another region keeps its MAC address, so the ELI and SAI quadrants, governed by IEEE 802c rules, are more appropriate for global uniqueness. For a VM that will not migrate, it is simpler to use AAI, because each region can manage its own addresses without checking for duplicates globally.
sections.eli5: A kid who moves schools a lot wants a name tag that works everywhere. A kid who never leaves can use a simple local one.

sections.title: Client-Indicated and Relay-Indicated Preferences
sections.content:
In the client-server flow, the client puts the QUAD option next to LLADDR inside the IA_LL option of its Solicit. The server walks the QUAD entries from highest to lowest preference and checks for a configured pool of that quadrant with enough free addresses. If it manages a pool of a requested quadrant, the offered addresses MUST belong to a requested quadrant. If it has no matching pool it SHOULD offer addresses from a quadrant it manages, by local policy. If it has a matching pool but no free addresses it MUST return NoAddrsAvail.

The client SHOULD NOT pick a server that does not advertise an address in the requested quadrants. It repeats the QUAD option in its Request and Renew, so that if the server cannot extend the existing addresses, the preference is known for new ones. The client SHOULD check that the received address is in a requested quadrant, and MAY retry with another server.

In the relay flow, the relay adds the QUAD option to the Relay-forward message, based on local knowledge such as a network served only by IoT devices. The server SHOULD apply the relay's QUAD option to all of the client's IA_LLs, unless configured otherwise. If both the client and the relay supply a QUAD option, the server SHOULD have a parameter to choose which one to process, and the RECOMMENDED default is the client's instance.
sections.eli5: You can tell the office your favorite bucket yourself, or a hall monitor can say it for you. If both speak up, the office listens to you by default.

sections.title: The QUAD Option
sections.content:
The QUAD option has option code 140 (OPTION_SLAP_QUAD). It MUST be carried either in the IA_LL-options field of an IA_LL option or in a Relay-forward message. After the code and option-len come pairs of one-byte fields: a quadrant identifier and a preference. The quadrant identifiers are 0 for AAI, 1 for ELI, 2 for the quadrant reserved by IEEE, and 3 for SAI. A higher preference value means a more preferred quadrant.

A quadrant MUST appear at most once; if repeated, only the first occurrence is processed and the rest MUST be ignored by the server. If several quadrants share the same preference, the server MAY choose among them. Pairs need not be in any particular order, so servers MUST NOT assume the first pair is the most preferred unless there is only one pair.

If the server cannot match any requested quadrant, or has a pool but no free addresses, it MUST return NoAddrsAvail. A client or relay that is unsure about the server's pools SHOULD list all quadrants, which makes a QUAD-aware server behave like one without QUAD support.
sections.eli5: It is a short ranked wish list: each zone gets a score, and the office tries the highest score first.

sections.title: IANA and Security Considerations
sections.content:
IANA assigned option code 140, OPTION_SLAP_QUAD, in the DHCPv6 "Option Codes" subregistry. The entry is marked Client ORO: No and Singleton Option: Yes.

The security section adds nothing new. It points to RFC 8415 and RFC 7227 for DHCPv6 security and privacy considerations, to RFC 8200 for IPv6, and to RFC 8947 for the security of link-layer address assignment over DHCP.
sections.eli5: The new wish list does not add new dangers of its own. The safety rules are the same ones the earlier documents already describe.

sections.title: Example Uses of Quadrant Selection
sections.content:
The appendix sketches how a device could decide on a quadrant. An IoT device might consider deployment size, mobility, whether it is managed, and its expected lifetime. In small deployments such as homes the device might simply use AAI, while thousands of devices in industrial or rural settings might use ELI or SAI. A device that moves might prefer SAI or AAI to limit collisions on other networks, and a fixed device is probably best served by ELI.

For a laptop or phone, the appendix lists context such as network type, trust, whether the network is new, location, mobility and OS network profile. A device moving through a public network such as an airport might use SAI or AAI, while a fixed device on a trusted work network might use ELI. Changing the quadrant could also make location tracking harder.

For a hypervisor, the choice might depend on whether the VM is migratable and on how it is connected, since ELI and SAI suit migration in a large data center.
sections.eli5: Which bucket you ask for depends on whether you travel a lot, how many kids share your rules, and how private you want to be.
